Traveling for the Movies | A Complete Guide to the Filming Locations of Only Yun Knows

"The days of the past have become slower, cars, horses, and mail are slower, and there is only enough time to love one person in a lifetime."

Directed by Feng Xiaogang and adapted from a true love story, Only Yun Knows not only earned enough tears from the audience, but also showed the beautiful scenery of New Zealand without reservation. Especially in the filming locations in Auckland, every frame is breathtakingly beautiful.

🎬【Filming Location 1: Labour Party Monument】
📍Address: Search for the Labour Party Monument (Michael Joseph Savage Memorial Park) directly on Google map
🚗Transportation: Starting from the city, it is convenient and free to drive by yourself; it is also convenient to take a taxi; if you take the bus, TMK bus goes directly, which takes about 20 minutes. After getting off the bus, follow the navigation and walk up the small hill. You can see the Labour Party Monument in a few minutes.
💙Features: Behind it is the magnificent city skyline and the sparkling sea, and the branches next to it stretch out, like a picture frame carefully crafted by nature. In the movie, the male protagonist played by Huang Xuan once sat alone on this bench to commemorate his wife after her death. Taking photos here is super photogenic, and any photo taken here is a blockbuster with an atmospheric feel.

🎬【Filming Location 2: Mission Bay】
📍Address: Mission Bay
🚗Transportation: Convenient transportation, easy to reach by all means of transportation.
💙Features: Aucklanders' favorite beach, sunshine, sand, waves, and delicious ice cream. From here you can also see Rangitoto Island 5 kilometers away on the sea. A five-minute walk up the mountain from the beach will take you to Michael Joseph Savinch Park. The blue bench next to it is the iconic scene of the film, which echoes the bench of the Labor Party Memorial.

🌟Travel Tips:

1. When you go to the filming location, it is recommended to choose a sunny day with blue sky, white clouds and sea, and the photos taken will be beautiful.

2. You can bring a picnic blanket and snacks and enjoy a relaxing afternoon on the lawn of the Labour Party Monument Park.

3. There are many restaurants and cafes around Mission Bay. You can take a break and taste local food when you are tired.

These filming locations in Auckland, New Zealand are like the continuation of the reality of the movie. Each one is full of romance and touching. Come here, follow the footprints in the movie, and feel the deep affection across mountains and seas💕

Smiths Bush is one of the six ancient forests to explore in Auckland. The Auckland urban area was once covered in lush, tall forest. The legacy of this majestic world remains in only a few precious patches around Auckland, many of which are easily accessible and well worth a visit.

Kahikatea forests are found in locations with high water tables, such as wet depressions and flat terraces beside major watercourses. These same landforms are perfect for farming and building houses so kahikatea forests have been almost entirely cleared from urban Auckland.

One of the best examples left is
is Smiths Bush, a green urban oasis of soaring trees and raucous tūī, right beside the northern motorway. Nestled within the kahikatea is a magnificent stand of pūriri.

The forest is almost rectangular in shape with very large, mature pūriri trees dominant in the centre. Large taraire, kowhai, titoki, karaka, tawa, matai, miro and tōtara are also present in the canopy.

Surrounding the pūriri-dominated forest is a dense stand of kahikatea . Smaller trees and shrubs growing beneath the canopy include mahoe, hangehange, kawakawa and several Coprosma species.

Pūriri is an essential tree to Māori, who use it for various purposes. The wood is durable and rugged, making it useful for carving, furniture, and buildings.

Parrs Park in Auckland, New Zealand, is a hidden gem that offers a wide range of activities for visitors of all ages. The park's playground is a major highlight, featuring an 11-meter tower with slides, a climbing wall, talking tubes, and binoculars, as well as an interactive water feature, swings, rockers, a merry-go-round, and a sand play area. Reviewers rave about the park, with one noting it's "one of the coolest playgrounds in Auckland" where kids will love the slide.

Beyond the playground, Parrs Park offers a plethora of amenities, including a cricket court, sports center, basketball court, and bike path, making it an ideal destination for sports enthusiasts. The park's walking trails are also a delight, with a 0.7-mile route that takes approximately 12 minutes to complete, offering a pleasant and easy walk through the park's lush surroundings. With its well-maintained paths and scenic views, Parrs Park is perfect for a leisurely stroll or an invigorating run.

Parrs Park has earned a 4.7-star rating from 12 reviewers, with visitors praising its cleanliness, safety, and amenities, including public facilities like restrooms, water fountains, and barbecues. Whether you're looking for a fun family outing or an active adventure, Parrs Park has something for everyone. Its sprawling 58.5-acre green oasis provides ample space for picnics, relaxation, and recreation, making it a must-visit destination in Auckland.

Craigavon Park is one of those places that instantly makes you feel like you've escaped the city without actually leaving it. Tucked away in Blockhouse Bay, it’s a beautiful, spacious park perfect for families, dog lovers, or anyone needing a bit of green peace and quiet.

The walking tracks are well-kept and wind through native bush, giving you that "forest feel" right in the suburbs. There’s a great balance of open spaces and shady spots, with plenty of room for kids to explore or dogs to roam in the off-leash area.

What makes this park stand out is how tranquil it is – birdsong, towering trees, and a real sense of calm. There’s even a fitness trail if you're keen to mix a walk with a workout, and lots of benches if you just want to sit and soak it all in.

Fairy Falls in Auckland is an absolute gem, offering a breathtaking immersion in nature. The scenery is truly magnificent, with a stunning backdrop of mountains, lush forest trees, and panoramic views that stretch to the city and the iconic Sky Tower. The highlight, of course, is the waterfall itself, a cascade of clear water that truly lives up to its name, resembling a graceful, white fairy as it plunges down. It's a unique and unforgettable experience.

I wholeheartedly recommend Fairy Falls to anyone seeking a peaceful escape into nature, especially those who appreciate the beauty of waterfalls. The best time to visit is during the summer or spring, when you can even take a refreshing swim in the pool at the base of the falls.

A practical tip: be sure to eat a full meal before you go. The walk to the falls is a bit of a trek, and the return journey, particularly the uphill sections, can be moderately challenging. Upper Nihotupu Dam in the Waitakere Ranges is Auckland’s second oldest water supply dam. It is a 50-metre-high concrete dam, 162 metres long at its crest and it can hold 2.2 billion litres of water. It was officially opened on April 14, 1923.

It was a hugely challenging project to be completed 100 years ago with least facilities, technology, and treacherous terrains to work with. Sand, cement and coal were transported by barge from Onehunga wharf across the Manukau Harbour to the wharf at Big Muddy Creek. It was then hauled 4 kilometres up the Nihotupu Valley along a makeshift tramline, and lifted by steam winch up a 640-metre-long incline and then hauled by a locomotive to the dam construction site. Construction commenced in 1915, and it took eight years to complete the whole project. Aside from a challenging terrain, there was a major shortage of both labour and materials during the WW1 time, and more workers were lost to Spanish flu epidemic too.

Upper Nihotupu dam is a gravity-fed, making it a 100%  sustainable and cheaper water sources for Aucklanders, delivering twenty-two million litres of water a day almost free. Not only it does not need electricity to pump water but generates power from micro hydro turbines that operate off the flow of water released for the wellbeing of downstream flora and fauna. These turbines, and solar panels, create enough power for its valve operations, communications, control system and lighting. Therefore, it is completely an off-grid plant.

During the severe weather event of cyclone Gabriella in 2023 the water mains that travels seven kilometres to Huia Water Treatment Plant were severely damaged in several locations and the dam operations were halted for few months to do the repairs.

Moore Park is a delightful escape, offering a refreshing blend of natural beauty and recreational opportunities. The expansive green spaces are perfect for picnics, games, or simply relaxing in the sunshine. The well-maintained pathways invite leisurely strolls, and the overall atmosphere is one of tranquility and enjoyment.

One of the most charming aspects of Moore Park is its hidden gems. I was pleasantly surprised to discover swings tied to tall trees far back in the field. They weren't professionally made, but they had a certain rustic charm that instantly transported me back to childhood. It was a simple yet heartwarming sight that genuinely lifted my spirits.

Moore Park is a wonderful place to spend time, whether you're seeking outdoor recreation or a touch of nostalgia. The park's combination of natural beauty and unexpected delights makes it a truly memorable destination. It's a place where you can reconnect with nature and rediscover the simple joys of life.

🚗 The main area around the car park is paved, and pushchair friendly. But also the most astonishing clear water with lovely little waterfalls and native birdsong 🦜🐦 I wish I had my togs (costume), because I just wanted to dive in! Smales quarry is recognisable by a sizable cavity in the ground on the edge of the water-filled volcanic explosion crater of Lake Pupuke. The quarry was once an important source of scoria and basalt. It is proposed to utilise the quarry pit for basement parking as part of a high density housing development for the site.

The original Herald Island wharf was built in the late 1800's when the island was called Pine Island which changed its name to Herald Island in March 1950 after a visit by the HMS Herald. There was no causeway to connect the island to mainland until 1960's, so the wharf had been a popular harbour cruise and picnic destination for people around Auckland. Now a popular fishing place, existing wharf was built in the 80's after a fire gutted the original historical wharf. It operates as a twin wharf model, one exclusively for Boat Club members and the other one open to the public. There are few car parking lots, boat hangers, two toilets, long benches plus a boat house.

Today, I wandered through Albany, Auckland, as the final days of autumn gently unfolded around me. The air carried a soft chill—just enough to hint that winter was near—yet the world was still wrapped in the warm tones of the season.

The path was scattered with fallen leaves in shades of rust, gold, and amber, forming a natural tapestry beneath my feet. With every step, there was a soft crunch—a quiet rhythm marking the changing season. Trees stood tall, some nearly bare, others still holding onto their last bursts of color, as if reluctant to let go of autumn’s charm.

By a calm body of water, ducks glided smoothly, their reflections rippling in the gentle light. A small group of pigeons lifted into the sky, wings catching the breeze, circling above before settling again. There was a quiet harmony in their motion, a peaceful joy in simply existing within this changing world.

Among the trees, a few stood out—perhaps fruit trees—displaying the final blaze of autumn’s fire. Their leaves, bright red and golden yellow, were scattered in circles around their trunks. It was striking to see such vivid colors resting on fresh green grass, as if the earth was celebrating one last burst of color before winter's hush.

It was a moment of stillness and motion all at once—leaves drifting, birds flying, water flowing. Everything felt alive, yet calm. As I walked, I felt grounded, reminded that even in the quiet turn of seasons, beauty is everywhere, waiting to be noticed.

Browns Bay Reserve is a fantastic coastal park located on Auckland’s North Shore, offering a great mix of relaxation and recreational activities. With its spacious grassy areas, scenic beachfront, and well-maintained amenities, it is an ideal spot for families, fitness enthusiasts, and anyone looking to enjoy the outdoors.

For families, the reserve includes a well-equipped playground that keeps children entertained, as well as picnic tables and barbecue facilities that make it easy to spend the entire day here. There is also plenty of open space for playing sports or simply unwinding.

The area is surrounded by a range of cafés and restaurants, allowing visitors to enjoy a meal or coffee with a view. The nearby Browns Bay town center offers convenience with its shops and local markets.

Parking is generally available but can get busy during weekends and summer months. Additionally, public toilets and changing facilities are clean and easily accessible.

Overall, Browns Bay Reserve is a perfect destination for a relaxing day by the beach, whether you’re looking for a peaceful retreat or an active day out. It offers something for everyone and is definitely worth a visit.

The Takapuna Fossil Forest is a geographical feature located along the coastline between Takapuna Beach and Thorne Beach in Auckland, New Zealand. It consists of a series of basalt rock formations, which are the result of lava flows through an ancient forest.

It is believed to be New Zealand's most well-preserved fossil forest in NZ.

Explore the fossil forest while walking the coastal walkway between the northern end of Takapuna Beach and Milford.

If you go at low tide, the remains of a petrified Kauri tree (New Zealand native) forest.

About 100,000 years ago the sea level was much lower and kauri, pohutukawa, and mixed broadleaf trees covered the coast. Around this time, the volcano that created Lake Pupuke erupted for the last time, covering the forest in lava.

The lava covered the trees, turned them into flaming torches. The trees that were not incinerated immediately rotted within the cooling lava, which eventually turned into a hard basalt shell. At low tide, the remnants of 500 tree stumps and branches can be seen on the reef. Perfectly formed hollow imprints of the trunks detailing bark and leaves are visible, some lying horizontal in the rock face and others standing upright. One of these, a 1.6-metre-diameter, 3-metre-deep kauri trunk, has been covered by metal grating for safety and is often mistaken for a well.

North Head (Maungauika) in Devonport is a fantastic spot for a family outing or a local adventure. The dramatic grassy slopes offer sweeping views of Rangitoto, the city skyline, and the Hauraki Gulf, and the historic World War II tunnels and bunkers add an intriguing twist.

One of the most joyful local pastimes? Sliding down the lush grass banks on a piece of cardboard.
It’s a simple pleasure—kids (and adults!) run up the slope, sit on their cardboard, and zoom down the hill with laughter and exhilaration  . Whether you're there at golden hour or midday, grabbing a piece of cardboard from home (or sometimes recycled from nearby cafés) ensures hours of spontaneous fun.

Past the grassy slides, don’t miss exploring the historic tunnels, disappearing guns, and coastal bunkers. The contrast of fun and history makes it a memorable outing—picnic on the grass, then duck into the atmospheric caverns, torch in hand.

In short:

Panoramic views over the Gulf and Auckland harbour

Legacy military structures and underground tunnels

Grass sliding with cardboard—a nostalgic joy for kids and inner kids

Perfect picnic and photography backdrop.

The Ernest Davis steps are named for a Mayor of Auckland and are situated by Logan Bank....which has more historical significance than the steps themselves being the remains of the home of Sir Logan Campbell...regarded as Father of Auckland.  In 1960, the site was donated to the public by a mayor of Auckland, Sir Ernest Davis (1872-1962). Still used as a reserve (2014), surviving remains of Logan Bank include a concrete retaining wall, garden features and in-ground remnants.

Some of the history is noted on an information board at the Ernest Davis Lookout situated at the top of the steps. The area is categorized as Historic Place Category 2. The path and steps link Anzac Avenue and Beach Road. Anzac Ave has significance as being one of the first roads in NZ to be constructed of concrete. The Anzac Road entrance to the steps is not far from the Copthorne Hotel and the bottom of the steps exits into the carpark by a backpackers hostel.

This review is solely for one particular staff member—an older lady working at the library on April 14, 2025, the first day of the April school holidays.

We had an incredibly disappointing and shocking experience today. My 6-year-old son was so excited to take part in the library’s pizza wheel reading challenge. He borrowed three books and was eager to start reading right away, so we found a quiet spot in the library and began reading together. After finishing each book, he proudly approached the front desk to share what he had read and get a hole punched on his pizza wheel.

To our surprise, this librarian responded with impatience and dismissed him, saying we were "supposed to take the books home" and only return later for the hole punches. I politely explained that we preferred reading in the library because it's easier for him to concentrate there. Her response? A curt "Whatever!"—right in front of my child.

It was upsetting to witness such rudeness directed at a young child who was simply enthusiastic about reading. It felt like she just didn’t want to be bothered doing her job.

Thankfully, I spoke to the manager immediately after, who was incredibly kind, apologetic, and reassuring. She confirmed that kids are absolutely welcome to read anywhere they like—whether at home or in the library—as the whole purpose of the program is to foster a love of reading. She also promised to follow up with the staff member.

While the manager’s response was appreciated, the encounter with this librarian left a very sour impression. I truly hope no other child has their excitement crushed in the same way.

Le Roy's Bush Reserve is one of the very popular tramping bushes in the North Shore of Auckland. You can either enter from Hinemoa Street in Hibury or from the Little Shoal Bay side and the loop track runs for about 3.5km. Generally considered an easy route, it takes an average one and a half to two hours to complete the loop leisurely. This is a very popular bush for bird watching, running, and walking. Dogs are allowed but must be on a leash. It has a nice canopy of trees with lots of interesting flora and fauna. It contains lowland forest with significant presence of kauri-tanekaha, broadleaved, and pohutukawa with wetland associations to the nearby estuary.  The Shoal Bay Stream is habitat for indigenous fish including inanga, banded kokopu, longfin eel and shortfin eel.

Le Roy's Bush was originally purchased by Edward Le Roy in 1918. He established three ponds where he grew water lilies and kept goldfish. After his death the reserve was purchased by a public subscription organized by the North Shore Branch of the Forest and Bird Society and has since been extended from the original block by addition of further purchases of bush-clad back yards. Now the Bush spreads into about 12 hectares in extent where it joins the Little Shoal Bay Reserve (7.5 hectares) and Lutmers Reserve (2.6 hectares) near Wilding Ave in Northcote.

Little Shoal Bay is a destination on its own, having a picnic area with BBQ, a small beach for swimming at high tide, a playground and over the road, bowling club, a tennis court and a basketball court.

We entered Totara Park from Everglade Drive, a quiet and convenient access point that immediately immerses you in nature. The moment we stepped onto the track, the sounds of the city faded away and were replaced by birdsong, rustling leaves, and the occasional splash from hidden creeks. The path was wide and well-maintained, winding gently through native bush and shaded by tall trees that offered welcome relief from the sun.

As we made our way deeper into the park, we came across several junctions leading to different walking and biking tracks. Signage was clear, and the trails varied in difficulty, catering to everyone from casual walkers to more experienced hikers and mountain bikers. We followed a relatively easy route, enjoying the serenity of the forest and the occasional open meadow where families were picnicking and children were playing.

Eventually, we reached the highlight of our walk — the Totara Waterfall. It’s not huge, but it has a calming presence, tucked into a quiet corner of the park and surrounded by dense greenery. The water cascades gently over rocks into a shallow pool, creating a peaceful scene that feels far removed from the busy suburbs just beyond the trees. It’s the kind of spot that makes you want to just sit and breathe it all in.

After spending some time near the waterfall, we continued exploring the park and stumbled across more hidden gems — wooden bridges, boardwalks, and small clearings perfect for a break or a photo. The loop brought us back to Everglade Drive with ease, making the whole experience feel like a mini adventure.

Totara Park is more than just a green space — it’s a sanctuary tucked within Manukau that invites you to slow down, reconnect with nature, and discover something new every time you visit. Entering from Everglade Drive was the perfect starting point for a relaxing and memorable day out.

I went for a walk around Wiri Mountain (also called Matukutūruru) recently, and honestly, it was a somewhat interesting spot. It’s not super flashy or developed like some of the other maunga around Auckland, but there’s definitely something special about it. You can tell it has a lot of history – it used to be a proper volcanic cone before it got heavily quarried, so most of the original shape is gone. But even now, you can still see old Māori pā terraces and there’s a cool lava cave nearby that’s apparently the longest in Auckland, but could not find it.

The area feels quiet and a bit hidden, which I actually liked. There’s a small carpark, which is handy – nothing huge, but enough space if you’re just going for a quick look or a walk. What caught my eye was this old shack on the site. It’s pretty small and boarded up now, but there’s something kind of charming about it – like a little piece of local history just sitting there waiting to be restored.

You can see the beginnings of some work being done – I noticed areas where they’re planting native trees and doing some cleanup. It looks like the council or some local groups are slowly working on improving the place, which is awesome. With a bit more time and care, I reckon it could turn into a really lovely community space. It’s already a good place to stretch your legs, take in some views, and learn a bit about the local history.

It’s not your typical touristy spot – more like a quiet, underrated gem with a lot of cultural value. I’ll definitely be coming back to see how it develops.

I recently attended an event at the event centre in Manukau, and I was genuinely impressed by the entire setup. The first thing that catches your eye is the building itself—it has a very unique structure that stands out from the surrounding area. It’s modern yet reflects elements of local culture, making it feel like more than just a typical event venue.

One of the highlights for me was the large Māori totem located near the entrance. It’s beautifully carved and incredibly colourful, adding a strong cultural touch to the space. It’s not just decorative—it feels like a meaningful part of the venue’s identity and sets the tone for the experience as soon as you arrive.

Parking was no issue at all, which was a relief. There’s plenty of it on-site, and even during a busy event, it didn’t feel crowded or chaotic. The layout of the parking area is well thought-out, with clear signage and easy access to the entrance.

Inside, the halls are spacious and versatile. Whether it’s a formal gathering, expo, or community event, there’s more than enough room to accommodate large groups without feeling cramped. The acoustics were solid, and the facilities were clean and well-maintained. It felt professional yet welcoming.

Overall, the Manukau event centre combines practical convenience with cultural flair. From the ample parking to the spacious interiors and the striking Māori totem, it’s a venue that manages to be both functional and visually memorable. I’d definitely recommend it for any large-scale event or gathering.

If you’re looking for a spot in South Auckland that delivers bold Mediterranean flavors, laid-back vibes, and a complete dining experience, Eastern Grill in Manukau is one place that absolutely deserves your attention.

Tucked away in the heart of Manukau, Eastern Grill offers much more than just a meal—it’s an experience. From the moment you step inside, the atmosphere is warm and welcoming, with the grilled meats, and baked bread instantly whetting your appetite.

The menu is packed with Mediterranean staples and crowd-pleasers. Whether you’re after a plate of crisp falafel, or creamy hummus paired with fresh, fluffy pita bread, you’re in for a treat. Their lamb is a standout—slow-cooked, juicy, and perfectly seasoned, wrapped in soft flatbread or served over rice. The chicken skewers are also incredibly tender, and the garlic sauce? Smooth, garlicky bliss.

But what really sets Eastern Grill apart is what it offers beyond the plate. They have a relaxed outdoor seating area, perfect for enjoying the warm evening air with friends or family. The vibe is social and unpretentious, making it a great place to hang out for a while.

Adding to that, Eastern Grill serves alcohol, so you can enjoy a cold beer or a glass of wine alongside your meal. And if you’re after a more chilled, social experience after dinner, they’ve got hookah (shisha) available in a range of different flavors—a popular touch that really brings out that traditional Middle Eastern lounge vibe. Whether you’re into fruity flavors like grape, mint, or apple, or something more exotic, there’s something for everyone.

The staff are friendly, attentive, and more than happy to make recommendations if you’re not sure what to try. Service is quick, and portions are generous—great value for the quality and quantity of food you get.

Whether you’re catching up with friends, going on a casual date, or just after a solid meal in a relaxed setting, Eastern Grill delivers on all fronts. It’s the kind of place you go once and immediately add to your regular list.

It’s a popular spot for dog walkers and runners - especially those tackling the famous 100 steps (if you know, you know!). Despite the lively atmosphere, there are plenty of peaceful moments to enjoy the tranquility of the surrounding trees.

Families will love the playgrounds - one near the main car park and another hidden along one of the trails. The park also offers a great café, tennis courts, public swimming pools, and well-maintained facilities, including toilets and plenty of seating.

This walkway wanders alongside the Manukau Harbour coastline, exploring the waterfront of Māngere Bridge township, before ending on the borders of Ambury Regional Park.

From Ambury Park, you can link up with the Watercare Coastal Walkway and continue on to the Ōtuataua Stonefields, along the Māngere Ihumātao foreshore.

The area is rich in history and natural beauty. Along the way, you will see evidence of Auckland's volcanic past, as well as countless native and migratory birds. You will also pass by New Zealand's biggest coastal marine restoration project.

I had the privilege of joining my son’s school trip as a parent helper to the Māngere Education Centre, and it was truly one of the most enlightening experiences. Although I grew up in Māngere and have walked up the mountain many times in my childhood, I never knew the rich history behind it. Māori history—especially the stories connected to Māngere Mountain—was never taught during my time at school, and I hadn’t realised just how much impact humans have had on the maunga over time.

The visit was incredibly informative and thoughtfully delivered. Our guides—Kimiora, Wayne, and Awatea—were knowledgeable, professional, very down-to-earth and deeply engaging. They brought the history of the maunga to life, sharing stories about pre-colonial life, the kūmara pits, pā sites, Māori ways of living, tikanga, and so much more!

Pakuranga Night Market is hands-down one of our favourite weekend spots! We love how you can snack, eat, and explore all at once. There’s such an incredible mix of food from different cultures—everything from savoury bites to sweet treats, all freshly made and full of flavour.

The energy, the smells, the flavours—it’s addictive. We honestly can’t get enough, and that’s why we keep coming back. If you love food and a buzzing atmosphere, you need to check it out. 🧡

“Saturday Night Secret: Pakuranga’s Underground Food Fest”

Pakuranga Night Market only opens on Saturday evenings — tucked underground below the Pakuranga Mall parking lot like a secret foodie lair. You’ll find plenty of Asian food choices: Chinese, Korean, African, and more. There’s even fresh veggies if you’re feeling healthy, plus cheap pyjamas and a nail spa for anyone wanting a budget mani (quality unknown, I didn’t test my nails’ fate).

Tried some food — not quite the authentic blast I get back in Malaysia, but hey, still good enough to keep this Malaysian happy and well-fed far from home. It’s no giant Malaysian night market with hundreds of stalls, but still worth the visit if you want a Saturday evening adventure.

The place is clean and dry, with a nearby toilet (important!). Overall, a solid experience — and perfect if you want to soak up some local flavor without the massive crowds.

We had a wonderful family adventure, walking out to Motukaraka Island yesterday. We initially tried to access it from Motukaraka Reserve on Puriri St, but discovered that the track from there is *closed*, possibly permanently. (The stairs down to the beach have been removed from the lower half of the cliff).
We then attempted to access the island along the beach from Beachlands Wharf (there are carparks, toilets and a playground there). We found this quite successful as an adventure at low tide for a family of adults and teens, but I would issue caution for families with very young children because there were a couple of points at which we had an awkward clambour up/down rocks at the base of the cliff and the beach can be muddy and slippery in places. However, saying that, there was a family group with fairly young children (and a dog) that came over after us and somehow managed.
The access to the island, even heading into low tide was muddy and wet (slippery in places). If you don't like getting your feet wet, definitely *bring/wear a pair of gumboots*.
Be very aware of the tide times while you are there. We left Beachlands Wharf about 1.5 hours before low tide and were able to circumnavigate the island and get back to the wharf by 30 mins after low tide.
The cliffs are beautiful, and there are some small caves on the seaward side of the island.
There is a single access point to the island's plateau: a set of steps beside the Motukaraka Island sign. These steps are fairly solid, but become increasingly overgrown with Cutty Grass as you get higher and the view from the top is almost completely non-existant, obscured by vegetation. We didn't persist beyond the fork in the faint track at the top, but we did see a couple Karaka plants with orange fruit (Note: the seeds are very toxic).
All in all, a perfect adventure for our teenage family. We would do it again!

Parking is limited and entrance is free.

I absolutely loved this gem of a place. It easily rivals the historical places closer to the city, with its park like grounds, plenty of off road parking & the volunteers who run it shared the history of the place. It was wonderful to see the huge old trees, & the old fruit trees as well, with the farm machinery & everything you’d need for survival on such a place. An out-of-the way museum with a very assorted collection on display. Several rooms are open that are roughly as follows: education and technology (so that has typewriters and cameras and radios), a household room (kitchen, laundry, medicine cupboard items), war (world wars and Scouts), sports and community, bedroom (items from assorted eras). Plenty of local photographs, some of which are photocopies, line the walls. Very modest entry fee of $3. Limited parking, but as there are so few visitors it seems not a lot is needed. Some items on display in the sheds or stable/garage but don't appear to be organised. No wheelchair entrance or path to the door. Most of the displays are upstairs so you have to be mobile enough to manage stairs. Staffed by informed volunteers and members of the local historical society. Well worth talking to them to walk you through the displays and for background information.

I used to maintain the outside area' for the council a few years back. It has history!  "the place' especially with no one around has got that eary quiteness about it" a cool place, the long drop is a blast from the past too, classic old school!! Worth a visit if your in the area"

Crystal clear water, soft breeze, and more shells than a souvenir shop. The toilets are surprisingly clean, which is a big win if you’ve been road-tripping on caffeine and regrets. There’s a campground too (not sure if it's free or paid, though — I wasn’t in tent mode).

I didn’t make it to the wharf on the other side of the mountain — it was getting dark and I value my ankles. Just had a quick stopover, soaked in the beauty, and zero regrets.
Also, plenty of free parking and barely a crowd. Almost felt like I had the place to myself.

One of the most interesting, exciting, and beautiful places to visit features a dam, a campground, diverse bird species, a suspension loop bridge, and excellent hiking trails. The dam offers stunning views and serves as a striking landmark within the area. The nearby campground provides a perfect base for outdoor adventures, with facilities that cater to both tent campers and those with RVs.

Bird watchers will be thrilled by the variety of bird species that can be spotted in the area, making it a prime location for birding. The suspension loop bridge not only offers breathtaking views of the surrounding landscape but also adds a sense of adventure to the experience. Hikers will find a range of trails suitable for all skill levels, from easy walks to challenging treks that reward with panoramic vistas.

This destination is perfect for those who love nature and outdoor activities, offering something for everyone to enjoy. Whether you're there to relax in the campground, explore the trails, or simply take in the natural beauty, it's a place that promises unforgettable memories.

I visited Farmers recently to return a t-shirt that didn’t fit. The first rep, Aruna, was clear in her communication and explained my options. Because it was a sale item, a refund wasn’t possible, but she let me know I could either receive store credit or exchange it for another piece. Since the size I wanted wasn’t available, I opted for store credit.

While browsing the sale rack, I picked out some more items. At checkout, one sweater from the sale rack scanned at $55.99. I had seen a lower price on the tag, but when another rep said it wasn’t a sale item, I wasn’t so sure anymore. What struck me as odd was that he came from behind the counter to the customer side to check the product, which felt unusual and left me second-guessing the situation.

What added to the confusion was being told that, since the gift card had already been swiped, the sweater couldn’t be removed from the transaction. Another staff member even suggested the manager could be called to sort it out, but the rep assisting me insisted it wasn’t possible. This was especially confusing because if the sweater truly wasn’t a sale item, then it should have been eligible for a refund — as I was told only sale items were excluded — or at the very least could have been removed from the transaction, since I hadn’t completed payment yet.

In the end, I opted for store credit, but the process felt inconsistent and left me uncomfortable. I’ve visited Farmers many times before and usually had great experiences with the reps, but this particular visit felt off.

My feedback: more consistent staff training and clearer communication would go a long way in avoiding confusion, ensuring customers feel confident about store policies, and creating a more positive shopping experience.

Woolworths Mt Eden is a friendly, well-kept neighbourhood supermarket that thrives on convenience and community charm. Located near the bustling Mt Eden Village, it’s perfect for popping in on your way to work or collecting a few essentials during a day out. The store may be modest in size compared to larger suburban outlets, but its layout feels spacious and intuitive—aisles are tidy, well-labeled, and optimized for quick browsing.

The fresh produce section is consistently good: crisp leafy greens, colourful seasonal fruit, and regularly refreshed stock. You won’t find the vast variety of a big-box store, but what’s available is usually fresh and thoughtfully curated. The meat and deli counters offer everyday cuts and deli favourites; again, nothing extravagant, but reliable and sufficient for most household meals. The bakery offers a friendly selection—classic loaves, rolls, snacks—sometimes including locally made goodies that reflect Mt Eden’s diverse tastes.

Customer service is one of Mt Eden’s strengths: staff often greet you with a smile or a friendly “Hi!” and are quick to help, whether you’re at the checkout or have a question about a product. The self-checkout area runs smoothly, and there’s usually someone nearby to assist if needed. Security presence is minimal—not intrusive, but effective in maintaining a calm environment.

Pricing aligns with other Woolworths stores, and regular specials (via app or in-store flyers) mean you can still snag good deals in this central location. Parking is limited compared to suburban supermarkets, but street parking and the nearby village car parks make it manageable—just a little planning helps during peak evening hours or weekends.

Overall, Woolworths Mt Eden might be smaller than its outskirts counterparts, but its combination of quality produce, friendly service, and convenient village location makes it a terrific option for residents and visitors alike.

Clendon Park Shopping Centre – Honest Review

Clendon Shopping Centre has the basics, but let’s be real — it’s seen better days. The centre has a bit of a dingy feel overall, and the atmosphere can be off-putting at times. There’s often a noticeable presence of homeless people and loitering groups, especially around the entrances and car park. A big part of this is likely due to the WINZ office on site, which brings a steady flow of people through the area — many of whom seem to be just hanging around rather than shopping.

The centre attracts a mix of locals, including many on government assistance, and while there’s nothing wrong with that, the environment can sometimes feel a bit rough or neglected. There’s not much security visible, and it doesn’t always feel like the safest place to shop, especially in the evenings.

That said, it’s not all bad. There are three real drawcards that keep this place alive:
•	Pak’nSave – for affordable groceries and bulk shopping.
•	The Warehouse – for cheap home goods, clothing, and essentials.
•	McDonald’s – one of the few modern, well-kept spots in the area, and a go-to for a quick meal or coffee.

Everything else feels pretty tired, from the outdated shopfronts to the general lack of cleanliness. The upcoming food court upgrade might help improve things, but it needs more than just new eateries — it needs better management, security, and a serious clean-up.

Unless you’re here for Pak’nSave, The Warehouse, or a quick stop at Maccas, there’s not much reason to hang around.

Woolworths Greenlane is a dependable neighbourhood supermarket that blends convenience with a friendly, community-focused feel. Nestled in one of Auckland’s inner suburbs, it’s well-located for locals and even commuters who weave it into their daily routines. The store space is compact yet well organized—aisles are tidy and easy to navigate, making it simple to find staples without getting lost. It may not have the open expanses of a mega-chain store, but it’s thoughtfully laid out to maximize efficiency.

The fresh produce section often delivers crisp, colourful vegetables and fruits. While choices can be slightly limited compared to bigger stores, what’s there tends to be high quality and consistently rotated. The meat and deli counters are modest but steady: nothing flashy, but reliably stocked with everyday cuts, small-batch deli items, and pre-prepared options for quick dinners. The bakery corner offers a practical range—breads, rolls, and pastries—sometimes with a few local favourites thrown in.

Customer service at Greenlane is a highlight—staff are approachable, often remembering regular customers and greeting them by name. Self-checkout is available and usually runs smoothly, although there’s always someone nearby to help if necessary. The modest security presence keeps things feeling safe without ever feeling overbearing.

Pricing is in line with other Woolworths locations, and keeping an eye on weekly specials or the app can really stretch your dollars. Parking is generally manageable—weekday mornings are ideal, but evenings and weekends do get busy, especially with the surrounding shopping precinct nearby. Overall, Woolworths Greenlane may not have the sparkle of a flagship store, but it nails the essentials: friendly service, quality basics, and a genuinely comforting shopping experience that locals appreciate.

Pak’nSave Glen Innes is a smaller branch compared to some of the others, but it still sticks to the classic Pak’nSave approach — low prices, straightforward layout, and no unnecessary frills. It’s the kind of place you go when you’re focused on saving money and getting the basics sorted without too much fuss.

The store isn’t massive, but it’s laid out well enough to make shopping pretty efficient. Aisles are a bit narrower than in the bigger branches, so it can feel crowded during peak hours, especially in the evenings or on weekends. That said, it’s usually well-stocked, and they manage to fit in a decent range of products despite the smaller footprint.

Prices are solid across the board. If you’re doing a big grocery shop or trying to keep things affordable week to week, this place delivers. The produce section is hit or miss — some days it’s fresh and fully stocked, other days it’s a bit picked over — but overall, it’s decent. The meat section is basic but does the job, and the bakery covers the essentials like sliced bread, rolls, and a few sweet options.

Staff are usually around if you need help, though like most Pak’nSaves, you’re expected to do most things yourself. People tend to just get in, do their shopping, and get out — not much in the way of chit-chat. Checkout lines can build up quickly, but they usually move fast enough, and there are self-service options for smaller shops.

Parking can be a bit of a hassle depending on when you go. The carpark isn’t huge, and it fills up quickly during busy times. If you can, going during off-peak hours makes for a much smoother experience.

Like with most Pak’nSaves, don’t rely too heavily on what you see online — sometimes products or specials aren’t available in store, so go in with an open mind.

Overall, Pak’nSave Glen Innes is a handy local spot if you’re in the area. It’s not the biggest or flashiest store, but it gets the job done and helps keep your grocery bill low. If you’re after value and can put up with a bit of crowding now and then, it’s a reliable option.

Their home section is another highlight, especially for bedding, kitchenware, and seasonal décor.

Overall, Farmers Sylvia Park is a reliable, one-stop shop—perfect if you want a good variety without having to hop from store to store.

Food
Pad Thai: Serviceable but nothing special. It leaned average, lacking the punchy flavours of tamarind, wok-char, and balance of sweet, sour, and savoury that make a good Pad Thai stand out.

Mango Sticky Rice: A real disappointment, the mango tasted like it came from Costco’s frozen/commercial stock rather than fresh, ripe fruit. Sticky rice is supposed to feel indulgent with creamy coconut sauce and fragrant rice, but with flat mango, the whole dish fell apart.

Consistency: Across visits, the food feels inconsistent, some dishes okay, others very underwhelming. That inconsistency makes it hard to trust what you’ll get next time.

Service & Atmosphere
Staff were friendly and helpful, which softens the blow a little. The space itself is fine, nothing special, but functional enough for casual dining.

Verdict
This is one of the most inconsistent restaurants you’ve tried. The Pad Thai was average, the mango sticky rice felt commercial and disappointing, and the overall food quality doesn’t justify a return. Friendly staff and okay space aren’t enough to balance the uneven cooking. No reason to come back.

Aesthetic and Tasty Experience at Breadtop

Visited Breadtop at the mall recently, and it was quite a unique and delightful experience. The store layout is intuitive — you grab a tray and tongs, then walk around picking out your favorite items from the neatly arranged transparent glass boxes. There’s a great mix of both sweet and savory Asian bakery options, including vegetarian and non-vegetarian choices.

Everything looked fresh and was frequently restocked, which was great to see. The staff was helpful and even offered to warm up the buns for us, adding a nice touch to the service. The lighting and setup inside the store make it feel cozy and aesthetically pleasing, enhancing the shopping experience.

At the end of the store, there’s a fridge filled with unique Asian drinks, right behind a glass door — a great addition to pair with your bakery picks.

Prices are on the higher side, which is why I’m giving it 4 stars instead of 5, but overall, the quality and variety justify the cost for a once-in-a-while treat.

Highly recommend for anyone craving Asian-style baked goods with a modern, self-serve twist!

Breadtop’s coconut bun is a standout—soft, fluffy, and filled with just the right amount of sweet coconut filling. The texture is light, and the flavor isn’t too overpowering, making it a perfect snack or light dessert. Always fresh and satisfying.Overall, a Breadtop is a great go-to for a quick snack, a casual dessert, or something a little different from the usual Western bakery fare. Highly recommended for fans of Asian-style baked goods.

Pak'nSave at Lincoln is a solid choice for grocery shopping, earning a respectable five-star rating. The store offers a wide selection of products, and the prices are generally competitive, making it a great place to stock up on essentials. The store layout is well-organized, and the signage is particularly helpful; the bold labels on the top of the shelves make it easy to locate specific products quickly.

The employees/workers on the Thursday evening shift deserves special mention. They are consistently responsible and focused on their work, creating a positive atmosphere for shoppers. They are efficient and professional, allowing customers to browse and shop without unnecessary interruptions.

However, there's room for improvement in terms of cleanliness and accessibility. On occasion, the floors can be a bit unclean, and there have been instances where boxes block walkways and hinder the movement of shopping trolleys. Addressing these minor issues would significantly enhance the overall shopping experience. Overall, it's a great place for groceries.

Pak’nSave Lincoln Road is a popular spot, especially with locals in West Auckland, and for good reason. It’s one of the bigger stores, so there’s plenty of space to move around, which already puts it a step above some of the more cramped branches. It’s got that classic warehouse-style layout — no fancy extras, just rows and rows of good-value groceries.

Prices are exactly what you’d expect from Pak’nSave — cheap. If you’re doing a big shop or need to feed a family without breaking the bank, this place delivers. You’ll usually find decent weekly specials, especially on meat, pantry staples, and household items. The produce section is hit or miss. Sometimes you’ll get a fresh, well-stocked spread, and other days it’s a bit rough around the edges. The meat section is usually solid though, with good variety and pricing.

The bakery and deli aren’t anything fancy, but they’ve got the basics covered — loaves of bread, buns, pies, lunch meats — all at reasonable prices. There’s a decent range of ethnic products too, which reflects the diversity of the area.

The store can get really busy, especially in the afternoons and on weekends. It’s not chaotic, but expect some crowd navigation. Checkout queues can stretch out, but they do move fairly fast. There are plenty of checkout lanes, including self-service ones, which help a lot if you’re just grabbing a few things.

Staff are helpful if you ask, but don’t expect overly friendly service. It’s more of a do-it-yourself type environment. Still, most of the staff know where things are and can point you in the right direction if needed.

The carpark is big, but it fills up fast. Getting a spot isn’t impossible, but during peak times you’ll need a bit of patience. The entry and exit can also get congested, especially when people are trying to leave all at once.

As with other Pak’nSaves, there’s a gap between what’s listed online and what’s actually in stock. So if you’re planning your trip based on the website, be ready for a few surprises or last-minute substitutions.

All in all, Pak’nSave Lincoln Road is reliable, cheap, and well-stocked — just be ready for the crowds. If your main goal is value and you don’t care too much about fancy presentation or spotless shelves, it’s a good place to shop.

Woolworths Māngere Mall, located within the Māngere Town Centre, provides a convenient and community-focused shopping experience for residents in the area. Open daily with accessible hours, the store caters to both early-morning and evening shoppers. While it isn’t one of the largest Woolworths outlets in Auckland, the layout is straightforward and functional, with well-organised sections for fresh produce, meats, bakery goods, frozen foods, and pantry staples. This clear structure helps make shopping quick and easy, especially for those stopping in for essential items.

The product selection at Woolworths Māngere Mall includes a solid range of everyday groceries, with a noticeable emphasis on fresh fruit and vegetables, which are popular with locals. The store also stocks a number of multicultural and Pacific-focused food items, reflecting the diverse community it serves. Though the selection may be more limited compared to bigger branches, many regular shoppers appreciate the convenience and the familiarity of the store.

Customer service is frequently described as friendly and welcoming. Staff are usually helpful and approachable, creating a positive environment for customers from all walks of life. The store can get busy at peak times, especially around weekends and benefit payment days, which can result in longer waits at checkouts, but the atmosphere generally remains calm and respectful.

Being part of the Māngere Town Centre means the supermarket is surrounded by other useful services such as pharmacies, banks, and takeaway shops, making it a practical stop for multiple errands. Parking is generally available, and the area is well serviced by public transport. Overall, Woolworths Māngere Mall plays an important role in the daily routines of locals, offering a straightforward, dependable, and culturally attuned shopping experience.

Unfortunately, Countdown Māngere is just as tired and outdated as the rest of the town centre. The store desperately needs modernising — it’s small, cramped, and feels like it hasn’t had a proper upgrade in years. The product range is very limited compared to other Woolworths.

There are usually only two checkouts open, one express and one regular, and there are no self-checkouts, which makes the wait even worse. Outside the store, there are often homeless people sitting near the entrance, which adds to the overall neglected feel of the area.

You’re better off going to the Airport or Māngere East Woolworths — they’re much more modern and better stocked.

Pakuranga Plaza, formerly known as Westfield Pakuranga is a shopping centre in Pakuranga, Auckland,
More than 80 stores operating in the center, including the major stores Farmers, Countdown and The Warehouse,
The Warehouse itself is external to the mall, but included in this center.

History:
Originally opened in 1965 as the Pakuranga Town Centre, the mall was one of the earliest malls in New Zealand, incorporating Farmers and George Court department stores. The mall itself has been transformed several times since it was first built and retains little of the 1960s style it once had. Originally it was open to air.

Operations and rank:
In a 2008 rating of New Zealand shopping centres by a retail expert group, Westfield Pakuranga received three out of four stars based on the criteria of amount of shopping area, economic performance, amenity and appeal as well as future growth prospects. It was noted to have received a relatively high rating even though struggling with major competition from Botany Town Centre and Sylvia Park.

On December 10, 2012 the mall was sold to Ladstone Holdings Ltd and was renamed Pakuranga Plaza. The mall was resold in October 2014 to GYP Properties.

As additional feature, busway and bus station also in the shopping center, as an intermediate stop on the Eastern Busway. This busway is connected with Botany Town Centre and Panmure railway station.

Woolworths Pakuranga at the town centre is a convenient local option for grocery shopping, especially for those living nearby. The store is generally well-kept and clean, with friendly staff who are often praised for their helpfulness and polite service. Many customers find the late-night hours useful, and the layout, while compact, is easy enough to navigate for a quick visit. Online ordering options like click-and-collect or home delivery add extra convenience, particularly for busy households or older shoppers.

However, the store isn’t without its issues. One of the main complaints is around stock availability—common items like bread, milk, or fresh fruit can sometimes be missing from shelves. Pricing is another concern, with some customers feeling that Woolworths is more expensive than nearby alternatives like Pak’nSave. There have also been reports of outdated shelf labels, which can lead to confusion at checkout when advertised specials don’t match up.

The layout of the store can feel a bit cramped during busy periods, with narrow aisles and occasional bottlenecks near the checkout area. When staffing is low, long queues can build up, particularly in the evenings or on weekends.

The broader Pakuranga Plaza where the store is located has also been facing challenges. A number of small shops have closed down, and ongoing construction work around the busway and flyover has impacted foot traffic. The recent closure of The Warehouse has left a noticeable gap in the retail mix, although new pop-up stores and food vendors are starting to appear. Locals are hopeful that planned redevelopment, including new apartments and upgraded facilities, will help revitalize the area in the near future.

Overall, Woolworths Pakuranga is a reliable option for locals needing day-to-day essentials. It’s friendly, clean, and easy to access, but it would benefit from better stock management, clearer pricing, and a stronger surrounding retail environment to truly shine.
